(AP file photo) BUDAPEST—Prosecutors and investigators with Hungary's tax authority on Tuesday raided offices housing data servers used by former prime minister Viktor Orbán 's Fidesz party as part of a probe into suspected embezzlement and other crimes, a prosecutor's office spokesperson told The Associated Press. Fidesz accused the governing Tisza party, led by pro-European Prime Minister Péter Magyar, of seeking to use legal means to destroy it. Marianna Bodó, a spokesperson for the Bács-Kiskun County chief prosecutor’s office, said in an email that the raid was part of an investigation into the suspected misuse of grant money through Hungary's National Cultural Fund while Orbán's government was in office. The county lies south of the capital, Budapest. Six current and former officials have been charged in connection with the misuse of some 17 billion forints ($53.5 million) through the fund. They have denied wrongdoing. The officials have been accused of distributing the money in an opaque manner to artists and performers linked to Fidesz. Some of them actively campaigned for the party leading up April's national election. A regional criminal directorate of the National Tax and Customs Administration assisted in Tuesday's raid, Bodó wrote, adding that no further information could be provided “in the interests of the investigation.” Fidesz said in a statement on Facebook that investigators had launched the raid “without prior notice” and “with the intention of seizing the party’s entire communications system and databases.” “There has been no precedent for this in Hungary since the end of Communism in 1990!” Fidesz asserted. Orbán and Fidesz governed Hungary for 16 years until their blowout election loss in April. While in office, they were routinely accused of overseeing unchecked corruption, seizing control of Hungary's institutions and undermining democracy and the rule of law. After taking office in May, Magyar has taken action to dismantle what he calls Orbán’s “mafia” by removing numerous political appointees — including the president — and heads of institutions viewed as having facilitated Orbán’s autocratic government. Since their election defeat, Fidesz has accused Magyar and Tisza of “tyranny” in their steps to dismantle Orbán's political and economic system. Tisza argues it is using its overwhelming electoral mandate to fulfill campaign promises. Magyar wrote on Facebook on Tuesday that he was awaiting further information on the raid from prosecutors. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock Bahrain Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation Rory Carroll and agencies Sun 15 Nov 2026 13.03 EST First published on Sun 15 Nov 2026 12.36 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain , casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation. Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran . Meanwhile, in Yemen , Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz. View image in fullscreen A Houthi fighter with a machine gun mounted on a pickup truck during a patrol in Sana'a, Yemen. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets. At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security. US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz. Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations. However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. Map Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms. A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz. In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement. There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway. The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks. View image in fullscreen The US Naval Forces Central Command headquarters building in Manama, Bahrain. Photograph: Mcs2 John Benson/Planet Pix/Zuma Wire/Shutterstock Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East. Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage. The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter. “It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse. Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law. The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.” Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast. “The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement. The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route. A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.
